tours.name: The Ice
tours.blurb: Bailey Willis reads the Vashon ice sheet — the Sound as a glacial trench, drift combed into hills, and one deposit nobody could yet explain.

keys.cap: The Vashon lobe of the Cordilleran ice sheet filled this view about 16,000 years ago, flowing south with half a mile of ice overhead. Willis named the drift for Vashon Island in 1898, and Folio 54 printed the name every glacial textbook has used since.

The upland between the Sound and the mountains lies combed north–south — till moulded under moving ice into long low swells. Willis mapped the grain as the record of the ice's flow; the modern relief beneath this drape still carries it, ridge for ridge.

The Sound's arms are troughs the ice cut and its meltwater deepened — Commencement Bay drops to deep water a stone's throw off the flats. In the shore bluffs Willis read an older 'Admiralty till' under the Vashon drift: two glaciations, stacked in plain sight.

White clay flecked with andesite blankets the plateau by Buckley; the folio maps it as 'Osceola till.' It is the Osceola Mudflow — about 5,700 years ago Mount Rainier's summit failed and came down the White River as liquid rock. Willis drew what he saw; the reading had to wait for Crandell in the 1950s.

tours.name: Standing Timber, 1897
tours.blurb: Crossfade to Rankine and Plummer's classification — what was cut by 1897, what still stood, and the prairies that were never forest at all.

keys.cap: Pull the layer slider one stop back. The yellow southwest is marked 'naturally timberless' — the gravel outwash prairies. They were never empty: Nisqually and Puyallup people kept them open with fire for camas and game, prairie country the 1854 treaty commissioners chose to call vacant.

Red hatching rings the city: 'cut areas not restocking.' The shore timber went first, into the water and off to San Francisco; by 1897 the St. Paul & Tacoma Lumber Company's mills on the tideflats ranked among the largest anywhere.

Solid green from the Soos to the Cedar: 'merchantable forest,' graded township by township for Gannett's Twenty-first Annual Report. Three years after the survey, Weyerhaeuser bought 900,000 acres of the Northern Pacific's land grant, and the counting turned to cutting.

Both plates letter MUCKLESHOOT INDIAN RESERVATION across the White River bench — a few square miles set aside by executive order in 1857 after the treaty wars. The Muckleshoot kept their prairies open and their fisheries running through everything the century did around them.

tours.name: Coal for the Locomotives
tours.blurb: Up the Carbon River to Wilkeson, Carbonado and Fairfax — the coal and coke district that fired the Northern Pacific.

keys.cap: The Northern Pacific pushed a branch up from the Puyallup in 1877 to reach coal it had located on Wilkeson Creek — a railroad built to feed its own locomotives first and towns second. South Prairie was its junction in the hop fields.

Wilkeson, named for the Northern Pacific's board secretary, shipped coal by 1880 and baked coke in banks of beehive ovens whose ruins still stand. Its sandstone quarry later faced the State Capitol at Olympia. The mine chip plots the Survey's own adit and shaft symbols.

Carbonado, the Carbon Hill Coal Company's town — for a time the largest coal producer in the state, worked under the river itself. The folio's geology says why the shafts run deep: the Puget group's seams stand nearly on end here, folded against the mountains.

Fairfax, the last camp before the canyon, opened its mines in the 1890s at the very corner of the sheet. The rails ended here; upstream the Carbon runs to the glacier on Rainier that gives the river its milk and its name — carbon below, ice above.

tours.name: The Terminus
tours.blurb: Commencement Bay, where the Northern Pacific ended — and Puyallup country, where the treaty system began.

keys.cap: In July 1873 the Northern Pacific's commissioners wired from New York: terminus, Commencement Bay. Tacoma was a sawmill and a prairie town; by the 1890 census it held 36,000 people, wheat wharves and the shops of a transcontinental railroad.

The engraved estuary — sloughs, tideflats, salmon water. This is the Puyallup Reservation, promised at Medicine Creek in December 1854 and enlarged in 1857; by the 1890s the allotment acts were passing the flats to mills and rail yards, and the city filled the rest.

Puyallup, Ezra Meeker's town: hop roots planted in 1865 made this valley one of the great hop districts on earth — until the aphid arrived in 1891 and took the whole business in a few seasons. The 1899 sheet still shows the valley ruled off into its fields.

Steilacoom, the county's first town (1851), sits just west of the sheet edge, and the Medicine Creek council ground lies off the same corner. The treaty is six miles beyond the neat line, but everything it set in motion — reservation, railroad, port — is on this map.
